title: Embryonic folds arise from local differences in growth rate of a uniform sheet

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Embryonic folds arise from local differences in growth rate of a uniform sheet

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The foldings of the blastoderm that produce the neural and amniotic folds result from unequal rates of growth, local accelerations and retardations, in what is at first an even and uniform layer of embryonic tissue, in the way that a sheet buckles when parts of it expand or contract.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: the various foldings of the blastoderm, by which the neural and amniotic folds were brought into being, were essentially and obviously the resultant of unequal rates of growth,—of local accelerations or retardations of growth,—in what to begin with was an even and uniform layer of embryonic tissue.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter III, “The Rate of Growth”; topic “Embryology and unequal growth”. Scope: vertebrate embryos (blastoderm / germinal disc), especially the chick

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch03-03: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.71

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Modern live imaging and tissue mechanics directly expose the variables and allow rival models to be compared. Existing open developmental datasets and standard tracking methods can test the mechanism in representative vertebrate embryos now.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Use time-lapse vertebrate embryo images to map local tissue growth and deformation before and during neural and amniotic folding, then fit mechanical sheet models. Spatially patterned growth that predicts fold initiation supports the mechanism; folding without the necessary differential growth or better prediction by active bending alone refutes it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Amniotic-fold coverage is less abundant than neural-fold imaging.

Growth, cell-shape change and active contractility can be difficult to separate.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.7
data adequacy: 0.6
data existence: 0.7
analysis feasibility: 0.7
operationalizability: 0.85

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Unequal growth versus active bending is a genuine contrast, and chick and mouse embryos have been imaged in ways that can locate folds relative to expansion. Those maps are not a single open resource matched to neural and amniotic folds, and the two mechanisms co-occur. A small team could reanalyse a few published datasets, which tests the chick-centered case rather than vertebrate embryos in general.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Map local expansion rate across the blastoderm and compare it with the sites of neural and amniotic folds. Folds sitting where an initially even sheet grows unequally would support the claim; folds formed by active bending where growth is uniform would count against growth inequality as the essential cause.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Strain and proliferation maps are in individual studies, not in a general embryo archive.

Contractile folding can coincide with growth differences, so the two causes are hard to separate.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
